Most folks don't realize that technology is currently accelerating exponentially. Elon Musk was recently asked what he thought the future would look like in 20 years and he was completely stumped. Things are changing so absurdly rapidly that asking what life will look like in 100 years is effectively as good as asking what it will look like in a 1000!

Exponential are a strange thing because meaningful but far from insane improvements on a local level don't seem so outrageous. But let's say the level of something doubles each year. It starts at 1. The next year it's 2, the year after it's 4 and so on. What is it after 20 years? It's more than a million. What about after 50 years? It's now ~1,130,000,000,000,000. After 100 years? 1,300,000,000,000,000,000,000,000,000,000.

There's a fable that a mathematician in ancient times gained effectively infinite wealth from a king by playing this game. In exchange for a service rendered he requested a simple payment. He placed a single grain of rice on the first square of a chessboard. And two on the second, and 4 on the third. He asked simply for a repayment of rice sufficient to complete this for the entire board. The king immediately agreed to this 'petty' request without realizing he just gave him every grain of rice the country would produce for many millennia.
The danger of extrapolating (even just linearly) when there are feedback mechanisms: http://imgs.xkcd.com/comics/extrapolating.png

Xkcd, like usual, misses the point in a failed attempt to be witty. One of the easiest ways to determine exponential growth for things that are not easily quantified is to look at an educated individuals expectations for benchmarks over lengthy periods of time vs when reality meets them. I think a nice example Elon gave was in self driving vehicles. In 2000 and before you might have said something like 2050 for fully autonomous vehicle technology. 5 years later you think well maybe 2040 and then 5 years later you're thinking maybe 2030. And now in 2015 we're looking at 2018-2020 for fully autonomous vehicles. The technology is advancing far faster than most any educated individual was predicting which is indicative of an accelerating rate of technological gain.

The more meaningful concern is that we're simply in a sigmoid curve with technology and not a true exponential but for now at least there's no real reason to expect this is the case.
